headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: kotaemon can ingest untrusted documents while xonsh can execute shell actions from its outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: kotaemon ingests documents, PDFs, HTML, and chat transcripts, so attacker-controlled content can enter its outputs; xonsh consumes shell commands and stdin/stdout, creating a plausible bridge if those outputs are copied or piped into it. No shared MCP or clipboard is documented, so this is not high, but the interaction exists in default workflows.
conditions: IF kotaemon output is copied into xonsh as shell text
IF a document ingested by kotaemon contains instruction-like content
IF xonsh is used to execute commands derived from assistant output
mitigations: Use a strict copy/paste boundary and never paste raw model output into xonsh
Add a human review step before any shell execution
Strip instructions from ingested documents before indexing
Run xonsh in a separate terminal profile with no auto-paste
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to kotaemon outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: kotaemon handles API keys and broad document classes, while xonsh can read filesystem contents and environment variables and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or environment, sensitive material touched by kotaemon can be exposed through xonsh commands or outbound requests. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF both agents run in the same filesystem tree
IF xonsh receives the same environment variables as kotaemon
IF files under ./ktem_app_data are readable from xonsh
mitigations: Store secrets outside any shared workspace
Restrict xonsh to a minimal environment
Separate the agents into different OS users
Audit shared directories for API keys
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: kotaemon supports multiple instances and writes to ./ktem_app_data, while xonsh can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. If both operate on the same directory, concurrent writes can collide even though xonsh does not modify git state. The overlap is real but not proven to be default-shared, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF kotaemon instances are run concurrently against one data store
IF xonsh scripts mutate files under ./ktem_app_data
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Run only one kotaemon instance per workspace
Keep xonsh read-only for shared paths
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: kotaemon produces document-derived answers and citations, and xonsh can execute shell commands or scripts based on those outputs. That makes a direct path from generated text to downstream action-taking, with irreversible effects if commands are run unverified. The pair is dangerous by default when outputs are trusted as authoritative.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands derived from kotaemon output
IF kotaemon output is treated as authoritative without verification
IF downstream scripts perform file or network actions
mitigations: Require manual verification before execution
Log and diff every command before running it
Use a dry-run mode for shell actions
Limit xonsh to non-destructive commands
requires-engineering: add policy gates for command execution

E_compliance.rationale: kotaemon explicitly handles API keys and customer-support documents, while xonsh can expose filesystem contents and environment variables. If regulated or secret-bearing data is processed in a shared environment, retention and residency controls can diverge, creating a compliance gap. The profiles do not show a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is indexed in kotaemon
IF xonsh logs command history containing sensitive paths or values
IF the deployment requires residency or retention controls not enforced by both agents
mitigations: Disable shell history for sensitive sessions
Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Set short retention on logs and transcripts
Review data-processing notices for both tools
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
